doc: Capability extraction. The router turns a work item into a set of capabilities and only then into roles, so that 'modify the TypeDB schema' resolves to typedb.schema + semantic.modeling rather than to an agent whose name contains 'TypeDB'. A signal fires on the task text, on the paths the change touches, or on both; every firing signal contributes its capabilities. `mix harness.route --explain` prints which signals fired, so a bad route is a line in this file rather than a mystery. This file is an evolvable artifact: it is exactly the kind of thing WF-020 exists to improve, with evidence. Short alternatives are anchored with \b: 'authorship' contains 'ship' and 'auth', and an unanchored signal routed a TypeDB schema change to the release workflow before those anchors existed.

weights.doc: A signal's weight decides the confidence the route reports, not whether the capability is included. A path signal outweighs a text signal because the paths are what the change actually touched, while the text is what someone said about it. A signal that also names a workflow family contributes `family` to workflow selection: the signal has already classified what kind of work this is, and a failure verb classifies more reliably than a domain noun — 'the product channel crashes' is a bug report that mentions the product, not a world feature that mentions a crash.

confidence.doc: The route's confidence is the sum of the fired signals' weights, compared with these. They were 6 and 2 in Router.confidence/2 and the sum was never returned, so a `:low` route — which the UserPromptSubmit hook injects nothing for — could not be told from one a point short of `:medium`. The score and these thresholds now travel on the route and `--explain` prints both.

signals.note: Qdrant has a client in `acme_knowledge` and a container in `docker-compose.yml`, and until an earlier change only the container had a signal. So every mention of it claimed `ops.deploy` and `ops.ci` through `infrastructure` and nothing claimed the code, which is how `fix the qdrant client auth header` routed to WF-015 Release at T4. `typedb` has had its own signal all along; this is the same shape for the vector store.

There was no general performance signal — `render-perf` is visual only, so 'session_start costs four seconds' fired nothing and routed to Idea -> RFC at score 1. It carries no family on purpose: a latency problem can be a bug, a feature or research, and the `regression` signal already supplies the bug family when a failure verb is present. The numeric alternation is what makes it fire on a *measured* claim rather than on the word 'fast' in prose. It contributes `qa.performance` alone and deliberately not `architecture.performance`: adding the second tied WF-002 with WF-004 Research, and the least-authority tie-break then sent a measured defect with a known fix to a research workflow. Measuring a latency is a QA concern; re-architecting for one is a different item.

signals.text: regress|bug|broken|break(s|ing)?\b|fail|crash|flake|bisect|\bnever (start|work|ran|run)|does ?n.t (start|work|run|fire|render|load)|stopped (work|start)|\bfix(es|ed|ing)?\b|refuses? to (start|run)|will ?not start|is ?n.t healthy|is not healthy|\bunhealthy\b|no longer|silently|wrong (answer|result|value)|exits? 0
signals.note: The failure *verb*, which classifies more reliably than any domain noun — “the product channel crashes” is a bug report that mentions the product, not a world feature that mentions a crash. The longer alternations were added after real work items missed it: “docker compose never starts postgres” matched nothing and routed to Release, and “the gate exits 0 while scanning nothing” is the most important kind of bug this repository has and contained none of the original seven words. `refuses to start` / `will not start` / `is not healthy` were added by an earlier change for the same reason the earlier alternations were: `postgres 18 refuses to start on this volume` fired no failure verb, so it was classified by its nouns and routed to WF-015 Release at T4. The sentence above this one had already been written about `docker compose never starts postgres`; the list was short, not the principle wrong. `fix` was added by an earlier change, and it is the most common failure verb in this repository's own bead titles: 4 of 79, against 1 for `broken` and 0 each for `bug`, `fails` and `crash`. Without it `fix the qdrant client auth header so tests pass` carried no failure verb at all and produced a THREE-WAY tie between WF-005, WF-002 and WF-014 at two points of capability overlap, with no trigger evidence behind any of them -- a workflow chosen by whichever the tie-break happened to prefer. It is kept out of `infrastructure` and out of the workflow triggers on purpose: a verb classifies the KIND of work, which is what a `family` does, and a kind match is worth 4 where a capability is worth 1.

signals.text: playwright|end to end|e2e|browser test|walk the product

signals.note: `evaluator fence`, `allow-list` and `deny-list` are here because a fence is a security control and a change to what it permits is a security review, whatever else it is. Routed without them, an earlier change's work — widening what a dispatched solver may write — composed a team with no auditor in it.

No `family` since an earlier change's second half. `release`, `tag`, `changelog` and `deploy` name where work is as often as what it is: "the release roles lack the beads tool" and "add a test for the release workflow's step order" both reached WF-015 Release at T4 with `git.push`, on family 5 + kind 4 + the bare keyword 3. The capability stays; the kind comes from `release-act`.

signals.text: \bcut (a |the |an )?(new )?(release|version)|\bcut v?\d|\bbump (the )?version|\bversion bump|\btag (the |a )?(release|version)|\btag v?\d|\bpublish (the |a )?release|\bship (it|the release|a release|v?\d)|\bdeploy (it|to|the release)|\brelease v?\d|\b(make|prepare|do) (a |the )?release\b
signals.note: The release family is a kind of work — cutting, tagging, publishing, deploying — and only a verb says so. `cut v0.4.0` fired nothing before and routed to WF-001.

Nouns only, and `ops.deploy` only. Two narrowings, both from an earlier change. The bare service names (`postgres`, `qdrant`) meant that naming a service at all claimed deployment capabilities, so a one-line client fix routed to WF-015 Release. And `ops.ci` duplicated the `ci` signal, which already has `.github/workflows` and `scripts/ci-local`: carrying it here gave WF-015 two capability points for work that mentions a container, and two is what beat WF-003 on a title with no keyword or kind evidence at all. The *verbs* — `refuses to start`, `is not healthy` — belong to `regression`, which is where a failure verb classifies the kind of work rather than its domain.

signals.text: harness|agent registry|subagent|prompt template|operational overlay|role prompt|routing rule|routing signal|gate lane|run ledger|conductor|dispatch|dispatcher|evaluator fence|per-run worktree|dispatched (run|agent|step)|environment (verification|verifier|suite)|session[ _-]?start|user[ _-]?prompt|pre[ _-]?tool|session[ _-]?end|harness[ -]?hook|resident harness
signals.note: The harness is three things at once, and a route naming only the first composes the wrong team: definitions that decide routing (governance.routing), a runtime with its own suite (qa.testing), and prose a future agent has to find (docs.authoring). It carries no family on purpose — changing the harness can be a feature, a bug or a doc fix, and the rest of the work item says which. The vocabulary is the harness's own nouns and it kept missing ones: "write operational overlays for the high-risk auditors" matched nothing and routed on the word "risk" alone. Note what widening it did *not* fix — that title still selects WF-001 Idea → RFC, because the workflow is chosen by the verb and "write" is not one WF-002 triggers on. The signal decides the team; the trigger decides the workflow. And the bare word `overlay` was tried and removed: "the HUD overlay renders behind the scene" is a Babylon bug, and matching it here staffed that bug with a routing engineer and a documentation architect. A design decision added a fourth vocabulary this did not have: `dispatch`, `dispatcher`, `evaluator fence` and the per-run worktree. "A dispatched run works in its own git worktree" matched nothing and routed on no signal at all, which is the failure this signal exists to prevent. `worktree` alone is deliberately *not* matched: this repository runs every agent session in one, so the bare word appears in work items that have nothing to do with the harness. The executable environments are a fifth: they are both evolution machinery and a `noetic-harness` command with its own runtime and tests, so `environment verification` fires here *and* on `evolution`, and the team that comes back covers both. That is the one place the two vocabularies overlap on purpose. The hook event names were added by an earlier change: work on `session_start` is harness work, and naming the event is the most natural way to describe it.

The executable environments are half of this subsystem and none of their vocabulary was here: "Environment verification reverse-patches the shared working tree" fired no signal at all and routed on the fallback. The bare word `environment` is deliberately not matched — a dev environment and an environment variable are ordinary repository nouns — so the additions are the phrases this machinery actually uses: `reverse patch`, `environment suite`, `environment verification`, `environment verifier`, `executable environment`. It carries no `family` since an earlier change. Every word here names a part of the evolution subsystem — a candidate, a benchmark, environment verification — which is where the work is, not what kind it is; with the family it made any sentence about that subsystem a request to *run* it, and WF-020 won twice at 12 of 12 and 18 of 19 for a defect fix and a feature. The capabilities stay: work on the subsystem still needs people who know it. The kind comes from `evolution-run`, which matches operating the pipeline rather than naming its parts.

an earlier change: the evolution family is a kind of work — operating the pipeline: evolving an artifact, acting on a weakness cluster, promoting a candidate — and only a verb says that. The nouns are in `evolution`, which has no family.

The verbs of *measuring* a candidate, deliberately kept apart from the `evolution` signal — which carries `family: "evolution"`, and a family decides the **kind**, which decides the workflow. WF-020's own note says it: touching the harness is a place, not a kind of work, and its intent is "when the same work keeps failing the same way". Widening `evolution` to match "a scoring attempt carries an allow-list" routed an ordinary implementation change to the workflow for a recurring-failure cluster, at trust T4 behind evo.promotion. So the capabilities are here and the family is not. Bare `score` is left out: a gate score and a test score are ordinary repository nouns.
No `family` since an earlier change: `promotion gate` names a part ("add a check to a promotion gate" is a feature) and `promote the candidate` is matched by `evolution-run`, which carries the kind.

kind_signals.doc: A work item's declared kind contributes capabilities regardless of its wording.

kind_inference.doc: A work item's kind is worth 4 to workflow selection and pulls capabilities from `kind_signals`, and until now only a caller could supply one — in practice only from a bead's type. A free-text prompt had none, and a prompt is what the SessionStart/UserPromptSubmit hooks route, which is most of the routing this repository now does. So a kind is inferred from the families of the signals that fired, when and only when the caller declared none. The precedence exists because more than one family fires on a real sentence: 'the product channel crashes mid-ritual' fires `bug` and `visual` both. It is ordered by how reliably a family classifies the KIND of work rather than its subject — a failure verb and an operational verb say what kind of work this is, a domain noun only says where it is. That is the claim; an earlier change is where it was written down twice and true nowhere.

fallback.doc: When nothing fires, the work item is under-specified. The router says so and routes to intake rather than guessing, because a route built on no signal is worse than an admission that the description is too thin to route.
